title: AI revolution changed nothing in trading, people are still trading charts
author: Aggravating_Diver405
selftext:
Hi there, just wanted to share my thoughts on the topic. It is hard to ignore that ChatGPT and Claude have changed the way we write code, communicate and work.

So it was logical to expect some kind of breakthrough in retail trading. But to be honest, I don't see it. I see that lots of people are still saying trading and mean charting, i.e. technical indicators, etc. And Claude and ChatGPT are used only to create even crazier combinations of these charts that would be proudly called strategies, etc.

I mean, trading is about data series, and the obvious and available data series are price data, bars and volumes. But the problem is that they likely have no predictive power. And even if they had, it would have been immediately exploited by professional traders and institutional players.

And for a retail trader, the opportunity may lie only in searching for market inefficiencies and opportunities in dark corners, by looking at alternative data sources, maybe exploring small niche markets not lucrative enough for the big boys. So I would expect that people would try to use AI to search for potentially interesting and trackable alternative data sources, like Google Trends, prediction markets, customer behavior (website visits, etc.), standardise them and try to build systems on top.

And some are doing this, but the mainstream narrative is still where it was, or am I wrong? I mean, I didn't touch trading for the last two years, although it is one of my interests, because I was focused on building other things. Now I am back and went through threads on Twitter and here on Reddit, and I see exactly the same crap: we are backtesting EMA crossovers and sharing our charts!!! In 2026 - what is this? It is like a time machine, but not to 2024, but rather to 1991.

What are your thoughts? Am I wrong and looking in the wrong places, or am I wrong and technical indicators and charting are THE thing? Or maybe there is no trading at all, the markets have become so efficient that no retail trader is able to extract any meaningful and stable value from them?

What are you researching, what are you reading and what data are you using? WHAT IS AI TRADING?!

comments.author: gnarly__roots
comments.body:
My thoughts: There is a massive separation between retail and quant level institutional trading at the moment, and it comes down to processing power, data architecture, and execution.

All institutional traders and quantitative firms have access to high performance C++ infrastructure, custom FPGAs, GPU clusters, and direct nanosecond exchange co-location. What would take even the most advanced frontier LLM models days or weeks to process, custom institutional ML models (like XGBoost, Reinforcement Learning, and temporal transformers) crunch in microseconds. But there is a nuance: institutions are not feeding raw numeric market data into LLMs. LLMs are terrible at raw tick math. Where AI and LLMs actually shine and where you are spot on about is alternative data. converting unstructured text (SEC filings, annual reports, earnings call transcripts, real time news, and supply chain data) into structured quantitative alpha factors. Retail traders often assume that advanced quantitative math or state models require massive artificial intelligence to process. In reality, the math behind Markov chains is decades old and easily runnable on a home computer. The real institutional advantage isn't the ability to run the formula it's having clean, high quality data and knowing how to calibrate the model so it doesn't overfit historical noise.

As for forward testing: while out of sample live data testing has been standard in institutional finance for years, what is brand new is agentic orchestration. Rigorous backtesting and forward testing used to require massive engineering teams. Now, a solid architecture can run agentic workflows to handle continuous forward testing, real time strategy evaluation, and dynamic rebalancing in live markets. Any time a new algorithm or signal enters the market, these systems can automatically rebalance to account for how strategies affect each other in real time.

I ponder why retail is still stuck backtesting old school EMA crossovers on Reddit and Twitter. 

A few key reasons I’ve gathered: 

 \-accessibility and literacy: Visual chart patterns on free tools are easy to digest, while quant pipelines require coding and statistical rigor and a lot more dedication then most care to give.   
 \-Overfitting: ALOT of the retail traders I’ve seen who try using AI, they usually hallucinate complex indicator stacks that lead to severe backtest curve fitting confusing historical noise with genuine predictable alpha. It’s very easy to match the past but incredibly hard to predict the future.   
\-Misunderstanding Latency: another wall we all sit behind on standard broker APIs is latency measured in tens or hundreds of milliseconds. Institutions operate in nanoseconds and see retail order flow. A lot of people think you can scalp big shorts. But you cannot use AI to out scalp HFTs on speed behind a standard retail broker pipe. You are racing a cheetah who can see where you are going before you get there. 

Where I’ve seen retail have an edge:  
the retail opportunity is not low latency scalping against the big players who control market microstructure. The real opportunity is using agentic orchestration to automate alternative data collection, parse niche news or sentiment factors, and deploy strategies on higher timeframes or in smaller, illiquid market inefficiencies that are too small for multi billion dollar institutional fund sizes to care about. The niche topic areas where institutional money is either legally locked out or too big to care. Things like: 

Special situations in micro caps: Automated tracking of biotech FDA calendars, tender offers, and corporate filings on illiquid stocks where a $100k trade moves the needle for a retail trader, but is completely meaningless to a multi-billion dollar fund.

AI-assisted strategy prototyping: Using LLMs to generate non-obvious correlation hypotheses and automatically build data collection pipelines that used to require a full engineering team.

The one I think everyone should use as a personal tool is Behavioral risk automation. Using a good agentic team to monitor your own trading logs, detect tilt or revenge trading in real time, and automatically manage position sizing. Most retail could position better with more accurate data, make more plays, and scaffold better. Which is directly associated to helping you design a personal strategy that works for you. 

I did use Gemini to summarize or better explain some of my thoughts but purely for organizational or verification purposes so I wasn’t misleading.

comments.author: Good_Character_20
comments.body: The alt data edge is real, but the thing that keeps it niche isn't imagination, it's point in time data. Google Trends quietly revises its numbers, web-traffic estimates get restated months later, prediction-market history gets cleaned up. So when you backtest on today's version of that series, you're testing on data that didn't exist in that form on the day you'd actually have traded. It looks incredible in-sample and then dies live. Institutions pay a fortune specifically for point-in-time snapshots of this stuff, and that's the real moat, not the idea itself. Charts stick around partly because price and volume are the one series a retail trader gets clean and unrevised. That doesn't make them predictive. It just makes them the one dataset you can test honestly for free, which is why people keep going back to them.

comments.author: AusChicago
comments.body:
I can offer a data point from inside the "trading charts with AI" camp, because I've spent about two years building a systematic breakout-pattern service with an LLM as the pair programmer. I think you're right about the symptom but wrong about the cause.

The AI never found me an edge. What it changed is the cost of rigor. Things that used to take a small quant team such as instrumenting detectors to log dozens of pattern-specific metrics, joining them with outcomes, running chronological train/validation/holdout splits with multiple-comparison correction, now happen in an afternoon. That's the real revolution, and it's invisible from the outside because the output isn't a shiny new strategy, it's a long list of ideas that *failed validation*.

Some honest numbers from that process: the edge in price/volume patterns exists but it's small. My best detectors beat the market on roughly 60-65% of signals, average realistic moves are 3-8% (not the 25-50% the textbook pattern-height targets promise), and the majority of "obviously predictive" features fail out-of-sample. The effect direction literally flips between training and validation, which means it was noise. Predicting a breakout *before* it happens, rather than confirming it after, is the hardest part by a wide margin.

Where I fully agree with you (and with the commenter above): the LLM should never be in the decision loop. In my system it does research, code, and statistical audits; deterministic code does all scoring and selection. LLM consistency is a liability exactly where you need reproducibility.

Where I'd push back: "no predictive power / instantly arbitraged" is too binary. Institutions have capacity constraints: a fund that needs to deploy $500M can't harvest a 4% move in a $300M small cap. That's a structural niche for retail-scale systems, and it's price data, not alternative data. Alt data sounds appealing but has shorter history and smaller samples, i.e. every overfitting trap of backtesting, amplified.

So my answer to "what is AI trading": for most people it's a faster way to overfit. AI collapsed the cost of generating strategies that backtest beautifully. The discipline to kill them became *more* important, not less. The EMA-crossover posts you're seeing aren't evidence that charts are dead; they're evidence that validation is still rare. That was true in 1991 too.

comments.author: Rare_Inflation3178
comments.body:
I think you’re mostly right, but I’d separate “price data has no predictive value” from “EMA crossover screenshots aren’t serious research.”  
Price, volume and order-book data can contain weak, conditional information—especially around liquidity, volatility, order flow and execution. The problem is that another transformation of the same close-price series usually doesn’t create new information. An indicator can be a useful feature or risk control, but naming five indicators and combining them is not automatically a strategy.  
Alternative data isn’t automatically an edge either. Google Trends, prediction markets and web traffic can be interesting, but they introduce their own problems: timestamp accuracy, revisions, survivorship, access costs and whether the signal can actually be traded after fees and latency.  
For me, the biggest contribution of AI so far isn’t “ask Claude for a strategy and receive alpha.” It is making the research loop much faster: finding and cleaning unusual datasets, generating testable hypotheses, checking leakage, building execution-aware backtests, and—most importantly—rejecting bad ideas correctly. The downside is that AI also makes it incredibly cheap to produce thousands of false discoveries.  
That has been my experience recently. I tested several volatility and high-frequency model ideas. Some showed strong statistical relationships but disappeared after tail exclusions, costs or executable portfolio constraints. A GBDT produced a positive rank IC, but didn’t beat a linear baseline and lost money after execution assumptions, so it was rejected. I’m now looking at a small market-making problem where the target is fill/trade-through intensity and post-fill markout, not predicting the next candle.  
So my definition of AI trading would be: AI-assisted empirical research and execution engineering—not AI-generated chart soup. The opportunity for smaller traders probably exists in low-capacity niches, messy data, market microstructure and operational details that are too small or annoying for large firms. But AI doesn’t remove the need for a real information source, clean timestamps, honest out-of-sample testing and realistic costs.
